en: Peṭakopadesa 4.
The Fourth Stage: Investigation of the Suttas.
In this regard, what is the investigation of the suttas?
Therein, wholesome and unwholesome states are thoroughly examined in their sequence:
"What indeed was this sutta undertaken for...? ... "Does it accord with those other suttas when their meanings are compared, or does it not accord?
Just as the Blessed One teaches the defilements at the beginning of that [sutta].
What has been taught?
One must investigate whether the abandoning of those defilements was taught or not.
If it was not taught, then wholesome states that lead to the abandoning of those defilements by the Blessed One must be sought.
Wherever those unwholesome states are abandoned. If,
while searching, one does not find them,
then those unwholesome states must be drawn out and investigated by means of the Discourse on the Side of Defilement, if the defilements are to be drawn out.
Alternatively, those noble path-qualities which they do not give there must be examined: do the defilements go toward abandonment on those stages, or do they not?
Furthermore, however many defilements have been taught, that many noble qualities have not been taught.

Wherever defilements go to their abandonment, those defilements that do not conflict with the noble qualities (ariyadhamma) as their opposites should be extracted, provided that their extraction allows for further application.
In this regard, one should investigate thus:
"Do two, three, or more than that number of defilements go to their abandonment by means of a single noble path?"
If, while investigating in this way, one grants a *yojana* (a measure of distance), then it must be scrutinized there.
Whether by oral tradition or by the transmission of the Piṭakas, the meaning and the non-meaning of the Sutta [must be examined].
Or, if it is impossible to point out the Sutta, then the Sutta itself should not be doubted.
Thus, just as wholesome states exist at the beginning,
those which are defilements should be abandoned;
they must be investigated.
Whether the teaching is presented by way of the wholesome or by way of the counter-factors, it should be learned without deficiency or excess.

One should investigate whether the first section—that for which certain defilements and noble qualities have now been taught—indicates that these defilements are abandoned by these noble qualities, or whether they are not abandoned.
If, upon investigation, they prove to be consistent with reason, they should be accepted.
Now, if they do not so correspond, those defilements that are not counteragents must be cast out;
and those noble qualities that are counteragents must be drawn forth.
For noble qualities do not lead to the abandoning of the defilements of a non-returner, nor do noble qualities conduce to the abandoning of all defilements.

Just as wholesome loving-kindness (*mettā*) is not unwholesome lust (*rāga*), yet by treating it as such, it becomes possible for the abandoning of unwholesome lust; thus, ill-will (*byāpāda*) comes to be abandoned through loving-kindness.
Therefore, both defilements must be examined.
Whatever phenomenon is pointed out, whether wholesome or unwholesome, that must be drawn out [and analyzed].

If they are consistent when being drawn out, there is nothing further to be examined—namely, whether two defilements are abandoned by one noble quality, or whether one defilement is abandoned by two noble qualities.

Or else, even if it is thus examined, it remains consistent; therein one must investigate how it is consistent, or one must investigate therein how the discourse can indeed be explained, for there is no room for doubt regarding the Sutta.
When the defilements and the noble qualities have been taught, I must examine them from both sides:

"Regarding these defilements that have been taught and these noble qualities that have been taught—whether by verse or by prose exposition—is it the case that these defilements are abandoned by means of these noble qualities, or are they not?
Or do these noble qualities lead to the abandoning of these defilements?"
Although unwholesome states are abandoned through wholesome states, not all unwholesome states are abandoned by means of every noble state (*ariyadhamma*).

Just as loving-kindness (*mettā*) is wholesome while lust (*rāga*) is unwholesome, yet it is not the case that loving-kindness is made the cause for the abandoning of lust; rather, lust is abandoned by loving-kindness, and ill-will (*byāpāda*) is abandoned by loving-kindness.
In this way, by treating it as a defilement (*kilesa*), it is abandoned through the discourse (*sutta*).
It is not the case that every teaching (*dhamma*) treated as a discourse leads to the abandonment of all defilements;
rather, that noble teaching (*ariyadhamma*) which is the antidote to defilement is what is abandoned by means of that discourse.

In that regard, when a wholesome discourse, Sutta, or explanation is taught, neither defilements nor noble qualities are logically consistent [with it]; these must be extracted by means of the component that should be demonstrated according to the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).
In that case, even if those defilements are abandoned through that noble quality which was taught alongside them, one must further investigate therein.
For what reason are these defilements to be abandoned, and for what reason are the noble qualities taught?
It is because in whatever manner the noble qualities are taught, in that very same manner this defilement exists.
Indeed, there is a certain defilement that must be abandoned by a specific noble quality and not otherwise; for example, wrong view, lust, and ignorance are to be abandoned by vision (*dassana*).
If this ignorance is indeed the ground for development, or the phenomena to be abandoned through development,

it is that very ignorance which is abandoned by means of the signless mental concentration and non-attention— the liberation through the vision of the unconditioned that pertains to the higher realms.
In this way, it should be examined both for its meaning and its phrasing.

The noble Dhamma has been taught in the mode of seeing for those defilements that are to be abandoned by seeing; the noble Dhamma has been taught in the mode of development for those [defilements] that are to be abandoned by development;
the noble Dhamma has been taught in the mode of utilization for those [defilements] that are to be abandoned by utilization;
and likewise, up to the seven taints, it should be applied to those [defilements] to be abandoned by removal, and so forth.
For this Dhamma is to be abandoned in one way, yet the noble Dhamma has been taught in another manner; that noble Dhamma must be sought in that other way.
If, while seeking this Dhamma, one seeks that noble Dhamma in whatever manner the teacher teaches it, then by that very manner the defilement is abandoned.
That [noble Dhamma] should be examined therein.
Now, if it does not fit, then a sutta established by that [other] sutta must be investigated.
It should be accepted insofar as it fits;
it should not be accepted insofar as it does not fit. "Surely this was not spoken by the Blessed One; it was [spoken] by the Venerable..."
Or it may be wrongly grasped, as should be demonstrated according to the *Mahāpadesa*;
and regarding that Dhamma taught by the Blessed One as it truly is—whether wholesome or unwholesome—the condition for that Dhamma must be sought.
For indeed, a Dhamma does not arise without conditions; there is no such thing as a "conditionless" arising.
In that regard, what is the mode of inquiry for the search?
Therein, one should investigate: "In such a way, this state (dhamma) has been spoken of together with its cause and its condition.
And that condition is threefold:
Mild, medium, and intense.

Therein, when the condition is mild, a mild phenomenon is to be grasped; likewise, this condition is twofold: the remote condition (*paramparā-paccaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*).
That condition, by its mildness, is to be sought as the measure of the disease.
What is the reason?
Even a single condition reaches fulfillment or completion through other conditions.
In that regard, whatever Dhamma has been taught, the cause for that Dhamma must be sought either by means of this [method] or by means of a reason.
Just as the condition is [to be understood] by way of the cause and the condition, so its outflow for that phenomenon is to be sought.
Just as one seeking the exertion in the exposition seeks it according to what has been demonstrated, so the condition is to be sought.
For there is no intense outflow from a mild phenomenon, nor is there a mild phenomenon as the outflow of an intense one.
Now, if what is mild for one who is mild, middling for one who is middling, and intense for one who is intense is appropriate, that should be accepted;
if it is not appropriate, it should not be accepted.

And whatever Dhamma the Blessed One undertakes to teach, he teaches that very same Dhamma from the beginning, the middle, and the end; just as he points out the factors in the beginning of a discourse, that very same thing constitutes the majority of the conclusion of that discourse.

Indeed, by virtue of that Dhamma, there comes to be that discourse, verse, or exposition—whether brief or extensive—as well as the two kinds of "establishment," namely, establishment according to suitability and establishment through teaching.
Furthermore, the "form" (rūpa) of the Dhamma is to be sought.
And just as the restraint of the five faculties was taught by the Blessed One for the purpose of subduing craving, it is indeed a desire.
Just as in the *Gopālakopama Sutta*, one should seek out that same teaching in other discourses as well, considering how the Blessed One speaks in other suttas—
such as those in the *Majjhima Nikāya*— thinking, "This is the Blessed One’s teaching in accordance with his method.
For a teaching is not to be seen in only a single sutta.
That which is being reasoned out should be accepted.
In that regard, what is "authorized"?
Whatever discourse was not spoken by the Blessed One but is nevertheless found within the discourses themselves—this should be remembered as such.
Regarding the statement, "As it was spoken by so-and-so," that discourse must be investigated:

Is this discourse indeed authorized and acceptable to the Blessed One, or is it unauthorized and unacceptable? Is some discourses authorized and acceptable to the Blessed One while other discourses are unauthorized and unacceptable?
Whatever the Ten-Powered One teaches as his domain without having to justify it in every respect—that entire discourse is unauthorized and unacceptable to the Blessed One.
There is indeed that disciple who knows the range of the Ten-Powered Ones both specifically and generally; yet he does not know that power in its entirety,
for knowledge through hearing is otherwise than direct realization— just as in the case of the venerable Sāriputta, who exhorted the brahmin,
for that venerable one lacked the knowledge of the specific differences between the faculties, and thus did not know that person from another.
When something further remains to be done, [the effort] has been initiated; that was disapproved by the Blessed One.

Just as the Venerable Mahākassapa exhorted his nephew—who was possessed of an immediate offense—by means of a miracle of psychic power, having set his fingers ablaze, [he taught him] the nature of all phenomena and the undertaking of kamma according to their cause and their ground, as they truly are.
Knowledge exists in that venerable one; he instructs him with it, and the Blessed One does the same.
"Even if you were to hold ten lamps, Kassapa..."
"He will not see forms;
his eye does not exist.
Furthermore, just as a messenger instructs people by the king's command, so too does one who follows what has been heard teach an unfamiliar sound to others.
A discourse that is approved and patient should be accepted;
one that is unapproved and impatient should not be accepted.
In this regard, what is the confusion of discourses?

The discourse is fivefold: that dealing with defilement, that dealing with purification, that dealing with vision, that dealing with development, and that dealing with the state of one beyond training.
One might accomplish one thing, teach another, explain the meaning of one discourse through another discourse, or explain the manifold aspects of the meaning of a discourse.
It reveals the meaning of the accomplishment of noble qualities.
It demonstrates the meaning of what pertains to the residual impressions within the context of the factors conducive to vision.
It demonstrates the meaning of the lower fetters within the context of the higher fetters.
He demonstrates the weak and medium faculties through the superior discourses.

Thus, this "discourse-confusion" refers to any confusion regarding the analysis of a discourse by way of its cause, its outcome, its fruit, its demonstration, its weak-medium-superior nature, and its meaning and phrasing;
whereas that which is free from such confusion is called "investigation of the discourses."
In this regard, here is the summary verse:
"The unbrokenness of the preceding [factors] is the condition for that which has come to be as it is."
The absence of latent tendencies, the faith in impressions,
the granting of permission, and the mixing of suttas.
This is the fourth stage of the Elder Mahākaccāyana, called the Investigation of Suttas.
